q: According to NSCP 2015 Volume 1, what term refers to the branch of engineering focused on designing and analyzing structures to safely withstand all imposed loads, including those from natural forces, over their service life?
n: NSCP defines Structural Engineering as the branch concerned with analyzing and designing structures so they safely resist all imposed loads, including natural forces, through their intended lifespan.

q: In mechanics, what term is given to a material idealized as undergoing absolutely no deformation whatsoever when loaded?
n: A rigid body is an idealization used in mechanics where deformation under load is assumed to be zero, unlike deformable/elastic bodies studied in strength of materials.

q: For which cross-sectional shape does the formula bh³/12 give the moment of inertia about the centroidal axis?
n: For a rectangle of base b and height h, the centroidal moment of inertia about the horizontal axis is I = bh³/12.

q: NSCP 2015 Volume 1 defines which field as the application of soil and rock mechanics to investigating, evaluating, and designing civil works, earth materials, and foundations?
n: Geotechnical Engineering applies soil and rock mechanics to investigate, evaluate, and design foundations and earthworks so structures remain stable on or within the ground.

q: Which of the following SI stress-unit conversions is INCORRECT?
n: A gigapascal is 10⁹ pascals, not 10⁸. The other three conversions (MPa, kPa, Pa) are correct as written.

q: A 100 N rectangular block rests on a frictionless (smooth) horizontal surface. What is the magnitude of the normal reaction developing at its base?
ref: Statics — equilibrium of a resting body
n: With no other vertical forces and a smooth (frictionless) surface, vertical equilibrium requires the normal reaction to exactly equal the weight: 100 N.

q: In the truss shown, every top-chord joint carries a 20 kN load and every bottom-chord joint carries a 20 kN load, with the end joints left unloaded. What force develops in member A?
n: Analyzing the loaded end panel of this Double Howe truss under the given joint loads gives a bar force of 20 kN in tension at the indicated top-chord member.

q: A simple beam spans 6 m and carries a uniformly distributed load of w = 1000 kN/m over its full length. What reaction develops at the roller support?
ref: Beam reactions — UDL on simple span
n: Total load = w·L = 1000 × 6 = 6000 kN. By symmetry, each simple support carries half of the total load, so the roller reaction is 3000 kN.

q: What term describes a structure whose unknown reactions do not exceed the number of available static-equilibrium equations, so it can be fully solved by statics alone?
n: When unknown reactions do not exceed the available equilibrium equations, the structure can be fully solved by statics alone, making it statically determinate.

q: A 6 m beam carries a triangularly distributed load that increases from zero at the left end to 60 kN/m at the right end. What is the magnitude of the resultant W, acting through the load diagram's centroid?
ref: Equivalent resultant of a triangular load
n: The resultant of a triangular load equals the area of the load diagram: ½ × base × height = ½ × 6 m × 60 kN/m = 180 kN, acting at the centroid of the triangle.

q: What term names the shear stress per unit of nominal bar surface area developing at the interface between a reinforcing bar and the surrounding concrete, arising from adhesion, friction, and mechanical interlock?
n: Bond stress is the interface shear stress between reinforcing steel and the surrounding concrete that keeps the bar and concrete acting together.

q: What is the term for the twisting deformation a member undergoes when subjected to an applied torque?
n: Torsion is the response of a member (typically a shaft) twisting about its longitudinal axis when subjected to an applied torque.

q: The ratio of a compression member's effective length to its radius of gyration (kl/r) is known as its:
n: Slenderness ratio (kl/r) measures how prone a compression member is to buckling; higher values indicate greater slenderness and buckling risk.

q: What term describes the transverse bending of an elastic member under a lateral force, found by multiplying the force by its moment arm to the center of moments?
n: Deflection is the transverse displacement of a beam under load; it is often evaluated alongside the bending moment produced by the applied force and its moment arm.

q: Which structural member spans over openings such as doors, windows, portals, and fireplaces, and can also serve as a decorative feature?
n: A lintel beam spans over an opening (door, window, fireplace) to carry the load of the wall above, and can double as an architectural feature.

q: On a stress-strain diagram, which segment runs from zero stress up to the elastic limit, where stress stays proportional to strain and all deformation is recoverable?
n: The elastic region is the initial straight-line portion of the stress-strain curve where deformation is proportional and fully recovers once the load is removed.

q: Which type of stress deforms a material through slippage along a plane parallel to the applied force, and underlies phenomena such as landslides and fault movement during earthquakes?
n: Shear stress acts along a plane parallel to the applied force, causing layers of material to slide past one another — the mechanism behind slope failures and fault slip.

q: What is the name for the location on a beam's elastic curve where curvature reverses direction and the bending moment equals zero?
n: The point of contra-flexure is where the bending moment changes sign (crosses zero), marking the transition between concave and convex curvature along the beam.

q: What is the name for a structural framework made of straight metal or timber members arranged into a series of triangles within a single plane?
n: A truss is an assembly of straight members arranged into triangular units in one plane, carrying loads primarily through axial tension and compression in each member.

q: Under increasing stress, what is the typical initial behavior of steel, being a ductile material?
n: As a ductile material, steel primarily deforms (elastically, then plastically) under increasing stress before eventually reaching rupture at much higher stress levels.

q: In the Imperial (English) system of units, stress is commonly expressed in:
n: In the Imperial (English) system, stress is expressed in pounds per square inch (psi), the counterpart to the SI pascal (N/m²).

q: What is the highest stress a material can sustain and still fully recover its original length, shape, and size once the load is removed?
n: The elastic limit is the highest stress a material can sustain and still fully return to its original dimensions once unloaded; loading past it causes permanent (plastic) deformation.

q: Which point on the stress-strain curve marks where strain keeps increasing without any further increase in stress?
n: The yield point marks where the material continues to strain under essentially constant stress — the onset of significant plastic deformation.

q: What is the general term for the contact resistance one surface offers against another when relative sliding motion occurs, or tends to occur, between them?
n: Friction, in general, is the contact resistance that opposes the relative sliding motion (or tendency to slide) between two surfaces in contact.

q: Force per unit area is defined by NSCP as:
n: NSCP defines stress simply as force per unit area — the internal resistance a material develops in response to an externally applied load.

q: What term refers to the unit deformation a material undergoes under an applied load?
n: Strain is the ratio of a material's deformation to its original dimension — a dimensionless measure of how much it stretches, compresses, or distorts under load.

q: Two planks joined by a single bolt are pulled in opposite directions. What type of stress develops in the bolt along the plane between the planks?
n: When the planks slide relative to each other along the joint, the bolt resists this slippage across its cross-section — a classic case of shear stress in a fastener.

q: A metal rod fails along a spiral, twisted fracture surface. Which stress is responsible for this failure pattern?
n: A spiral, twisted fracture surface is characteristic of a torsional (shear-dominated) failure caused by excessive applied torque, not by simple tension or compression.

q: The figure shows transverse loading producing both concave and convex curvature along the beam. Which labeled curve represents positive bending?
n: By the standard sign convention, positive bending produces a concave-up (sagging) curvature — shown as curve B, consistent with the beam bending like a smile.

q: In the moment diagram for a beam segment between supports C and D, what is the name for the location where the bending moment crosses zero?
n: Where the moment diagram crosses the baseline (moment = 0) is called the inflection point — the same location where the beam's curvature reverses.
